subsubtopic: CALL FOR CUTBACKS IN MEMBERSHIP-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:

That the federal cabinet be subject to an immediate 20 per cent cutback by order of this House requiring the termination of services by laying off Chairman Pierre and his ministers of finance, energy, transport, housing and industry, all of whom are drawing heavy tax subsidies from Canadians in order to finance their own reckless incompetence, and that public hearings need not be held until after these cuts take effect on November 16, 1981.

subsubtopic: IMPACT ON CONSTRUCTION OF RENTAL HOUSING
speechtext: In the absence of the Minister of Finance, Madam Speaker, I will address my question to the acting minister of finance. The minister said last week that his budget was designed to increase employment. The government's answer to unemployment is to create it. Since the budget was introduced last Thursday night, construction has stopped, just ended, on 3,200 rental units worth half a billion dollars, from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Vancouver, throwing 3,400 people out of work. When the Minister of Finance brought in his restrictive budget, was the government aware that these projects would halt, that these jobs would be lost, and that an entire industry would be wiped out?

subsubtopic: IMPACT ON CONSTRUCTION OF RENTAL HOUSING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member is concerned about one particular situation that affects homebuilding. If the hon. member would look carefully at the measures taken to counter inflation, she will realize that those measures are the most effective way to revive that particular section of the industry. In fact, if we succeed in bringing down the present rates of inflation which are affecting the economy, the result will be a substantial reduction in interest rates, and hence more room and greater demand for construction; this industrial sector will get back on its feet and the economy will benefit because more jobs will be created as well.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Minister of State for Finance, who has managed to enunciate what econo-

November 16, 1981
Oral Questions
mists call the enema theory of fighting inflation, by flushing out the economy.
Hear, hear!

The minister has not addressed the question which was about specific projects, in specific centres, on which work has stopped and in which people are out of work today. People who were working last Thursday are not working today. The Canadian Institute of Public Real Estate Companies estimates that the number of lost rental units will be in the thousands, at a time when vacancy rates are at the lowest level in five years. Will the Minister of State for Finance consider recommending to the Minister of Finance that he amend his budget proposals affecting the soft costs, so that these projects can now proceed and that these jobs can be saved?
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, when referring to rhetoric and the practitioners thereof, one can use all kinds of expressions. The hon. member has used one, and I would like to suggest another; I would say that she is indulging in psittacism, just like her party leader who made a habit of imitating parrots.
Madam Speaker, to get back to the basic principles of the budget, these are to fight inflation, to get interest rates down and thus create more jobs as a result of the ensuing economic revival. The hon. member is referring to several problems which might be caused by certain arrangements concerning obligations to invest in housing. This is a problem the Minister of Finance is well aware of. We shall have an opportunity to look at this more closely during the next few days, and I am sure that if it is necessary to take special measures regarding this particular aspect, the Minister of Finance will consider such measures.

My supplementary question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance who, in his answer, indicated, at least as I heard it, that the government would consider looking into this aspect to see whether these jobs can be saved. Since these people are now out of work and since all these projects are now on hold, when will the minister be able to tell this House what the results of this extra scrutiny will be?
Madam Speaker, I feel that there should be time to consider a situation or the consequences of a specific measure before we can say when a more definite answer can be given.

subsubtopic: ACTIONS TO MEET SHORTFALL IN MAJOR METROPOLITAN AREAS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the minister responsible for housing. The minister will know that on last Friday Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation announced that the vacancy rate in all major metropolitan areas of the country had slipped to 1.4 per cent. He will also know that this is critical in some of the larger metropolitan areas such as the city of Toronto where the vacancy rate has gone from 1.7 per cent in 1979 to .3 per cent in 1981, a very critical factor.
Given the fact that the budget eliminated the MURB provision which, by the minister's own admission, resulted in the creation of 20,000 units last year, and that it will be replaced by a subsidization provision which will only allow for the building of 15,000 units, what does the minister propose to do to meet the critical shortfall in major metropolitan areas of the country which, by his dire predictions contained in his own cabinet document, could result and perhaps will result in a black market situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: ACTIONS TO MEET SHORTFALL IN MAJOR METROPOLITAN AREAS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are two things for which the budget is designed in addressing the problems raised by the hon. member. First, I believe that he overlooked, in the proposition for 15,000 new rental starts to be encouraged by the front-end loading of the $7,500 grant, that those units now under the program can at last be specifically directed to those markets where low vacancy rates exist. Heretofore under the MURB provision, that was a helter-skelter approach. It assisted the industry, it got units constructed, but they were not necessarily in the areas where they were needed. I have been told that many times by hon. members opposite. The advantage of this alternative approach taken in the budget is to address the assistance where it is required, in those markets experiencing the low vacancy rate.
Second, I would remind the hon. member that I answered the first question he raised in this resumed session of Parliament that the corporation had already directed Section 56(1) units, which are a substitute to rental units, non-profit and co-op units, to those markets. We have increased the allocation in the last two years. I gave as an example the city which the hon. member represents where there has been an increase in that type of alternative housing.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the budget has decreased the supply of co-op social housing by 5,000 units; it has gone from 30,000 to 25,000. The deferred mortgage interest payment situation will not address the problem, and that has been exacerbated by a considerable decline in investor confidence in the market by the elimination of the MURB provision. That has created a critical situation

in the country. It will result in a black market situation in major metropolitan areas, the so-called key money situations. The minister has to bear some responsibility in this regard. What steps does he propose to take to monitor the situation in major metropolitan areas to ensure that the black market key money situation which he predicted in his cabinet document which he signed will not in fact take place? We are now approaching the zero vacancy rate which he predicted in his document. The minister seems determined to make his own worst predictions come true.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the first step, as the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation reporting to Parliament, that I will take is to meet with my provincial counterparts, the ministers of housing of all provinces. I requested that on Friday, the morning after the budget. I received confirmation from two ministers. I intend to meet with all of them in the next few weeks to discuss this very issue.
I point out to the hon. member, for example, that the province of Ontario has a comparable plan to assist rental housing by an up-front grant. We obviously have to work with that province in co-operation, to see that both programs achieve the desired element that is required in the plan. I was happy to see, for example, that last week after the budget announcement of plans in this House, and after I had requested that the provinces now consider what aid they would get, the province of Manitoba will pick up some slack and address some of its financial resources to the problem of housing. I will ask the other ministers of housing in the other provinces whether they as well can follow that leadership.

subtopic: TRANSFER OF SALES TAX FROM MANUFACTURING TO WHOLESALE LEVEL
TRANSFER OF SALES TAX FROM MANUFACTURING TO WHOLESALE LEVEL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance in the absence of the Minister of Finance. We all know that total tax revenues will increase this year by 31 per cent as a result of the budget. What is not clear as a result of the budget is the impact of the shift of the federal sales tax from the manufacturing level to the wholesale level. The government has said it will reduce the rate from 9 per cent to 8 per cent, but many experts in the Consumers' Association of Canada and in the business community claim that this will result in a considerably larger revenue take than has been indicated in the budget.
Is the government trying to sneak in a further revenue increase on top of this 31 per cent increase, a tax increase which would be very, very damaging as far as Canadian consumers are concerned in that it will raise costs and will also be very damaging to the level of unemployment?

subtopic: TRANSFER OF SALES TAX FROM MANUFACTURING TO WHOLESALE LEVEL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member's question is very interesting. However, I should like to point out to the hon. member that in the preamble to his question which is specifically concerned with the shift of the sales tax from the manufacturing level to the wholesale level, he forgot to point out that at the same time, revenue is being generated by the removal of certain tax preferences, marginal income tax rates have been substantially reduced, and nearly six million Canadians will experience a reduction in marginal income tax rates for next year, which is very important.
As for the effects of the sales tax transfer from the manufacturing to the wholesale level, the hon. member is quite right to express his concerns which I feel are well founded. In fact, the purpose of the Minister of Finance and the government in making this change is not to generate new revenue for the government. The government's objective is to provide for greater equity in the sales tax system, first of all by shifting collection of this tax away from the manufacturing level. This does away with a multitude of problems that had made the levying of the sales tax at this level a veritable nightmare for the Department of National revenue. Second, as far as the amount to which the sales tax is to be applied is concerned, the new approach deals more equitably with, and provides a better balance between, imported goods and the same goods manufactured here in Canada. The objective is therefore not to generate more revenue but to apply the sales tax more equitably.

Madam Speaker,
I should remind the minister that about ten years ago there were the same concerns as a result of the Benson tax reform. At that time the government said that if the tax reform generated further revenue increases than what it then anticipated, it would give that money back. Hon. members know, I know, and Your Honour knows what happened at that time. There were no tax reductions as a result of that. I am now asking the minister for a commitment on behalf of the government that that will take place.
The Minister of Finance obviously wrote the budget before he got the information concerning the high unemployment figures in October as well as the other very widespread signs of weakness in the economy. Therefore my supplementary question to the Minister of State for Finance is as follows: In this budget, why did the minister ignore the fact that today the economy is in a recession? Why did he increase the tax burden on Canadians by a further $1.4 billion on top of the $1,400 per family per year for the next five years that the energy tax increase will bring to the government?

I would like to comment briefly on the hon. member's statement, in view of the neutrality that is desired when levying the sales tax at the wholesale rather than at the manufacturing level. I can assure the hon. member that we shall have an opportunity to discuss the matter with the parties concerned at committee hearings, that the hon. member will also have an opportunity to get his points across and that he will realize, in the course of the debate in committee, that the change will indeed provide for a more equitable and objective system. As for the general objectives of the budget with respect to the economy, I think the hon. member will agree that the government's main focus must be on the fight against inflation. The hon. member may recall that 13 months ago, before the Minister of Finance had brought down a budget, a number of members were saying: Listen, we are in a recession, be careful when you prepare your budget because the recession is going to be severe and there will be high unemployment rates. Several months later, the Canadian economy had shown a quite remarkable rate of growth. As every good physician knows, a hasty diagnosis is seldom right.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise to participate in this budget debate with enthusiasm and with a good deal of satisfaction.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are the only one in Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about hope?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The budget tabled in this House by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on November 12 was by no means just an ordinary budget. It is not a budget which simply closed off a plethora of tax loopholes in order to provide more tax dollars to the government's treasury and, of course, to the treasuries of those provinces with which we have tax collection agreements. It is a budget which I believe in some respects represents a philosophical
November 16, 1981

turning point in the fiscal policy of the government, a philosophy which I personally have long espoused and one which to a considerable degree inspired me to enter politics in the mid-1970s.
Fiscal policy has long been for me a personal preoccupation. I believe that the fiscal policy of a nation, both on the tax side and on the expenditure side, tells us a great deal about the fundamental values of a particular society. I have long held the belief that our tax system, the one that emerged from so-called tax reform in 1971, has remained replete with inequities, anomalies and complexities, all of which I believe have served to weigh heavily upon the morale of Canadian taxpayers and perhaps to some degree even on the morality of Canadians.
I committed some of my criticisms to writing in a book on tax reform back in 1974 because I was convinced at that time that we were moving in the wrong direction. I believe that tax reform since that time has remained important. It is as important in 1981 as it was in 1971. The budget that was tabled by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, on November 12 is a very important step in that process of tax reform, a step which I hope will be pursued in successive budgets.

Mr. Speaker, there are many fiscal matters of which I would like to speak this afternoon. While I would wish to make a detailed examination of several aspects of the budget calling for a fundamental reform of our taxation system, I shall make only one rather general but in my opinion extremely important comment.
In my own experience as a tax law specialist and in the experience of my former professional colleagues in Canada and even in the United States, it is very obvious that marginal tax rates over 50 per cent have brought some taxpayers to look for loopholes to protect themselves against what they see as an undue appropriation of their own income. These loopholes have been used as much as possible because of the complexity of our legislation and of the tax burden imposed on our taxpayers. This is a way of thinking which I understand very well, Mr. Speaker, and I spent much of my professional life creating tax shelters or havens.
Mr. Speaker, can you imagine anything less positive than these efforts by professionals to make use of the loopholes in our tax laws? However, with taxation rates over 50 per cent, Canadian taxpayers will inevitably make every effort in this regard. I am convinced that, with a fair and equitable tax system where the rates do not exceed 50 per cent, there will be a significant reduction in the efforts made by taxpayers to evade the law. It is in that spirit that I wrote late in December 1976:

There is good authority for the view that a taxpayer's resistance to the expropriation of his income by government will increase when the tax rate exceeds 50 per cent. I believe this view has been reinforced through a recent experience in the United States where the highest tax rate on income at the federal level is now 50 per cent. Recently a U.S. tax attorney advised that with the introduction of a maximum 50 per cent rate, many of his clients have
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
abandoned tax avoidance schemes and are reconciled to paying 50 per cent of their earned income to the federal government. Because of this it may well be that more taxes are in fact collected where a 50 per cent maximum rate exists.

Mr. Speaker, that is one of the reasons for my satisfaction today and, before completing this secondary point, I should like to emphasize that the review of our tax system, an extremely significant stage of which is represented by this budget, would result in the elimination of those tax shelters and other kinds of loopholes so that our system will finally be simple and fair. This would also spur the innovative spirit of Canadian businessmen and the creation of capital, thus paving the way for an economic plan from which every Canadian would derive major benefits.

I hold the personal conviction that the taxation system is the single most important element of economic growth. That growth depends upon the successful marriage of capital resources and labour and that marriage can only be brought about by the efforts of our entrepreneurs, our innovators. The tax system must contribute to the formation of capital through appropriate incentives to save. It must be the principal vehicle that brings capital and labour to the resources. The tax system must be perceived as fair and equitable by Canadians and by Canadian workers. Finally, it must contain rewards for the risk-takers, our entrepreneurs who have successfully brought Canada from the wilderness to the forefront of the industrialized countries of the world.
I believe that this budget is in many respects a major step in the direction of satisfying all those objectives. It will contribute to productivity, economic growth, job creation and reduced inflation.
In my concern for fiscal reform, I am also riding another hobbyhorse, which was another factor which convinced me, and I am sure others, to enter the political process. I am referring to the other side of Fiscal policy, the expenditure side. I was convinced before I came to this place, and I am even more convinced now that I am here, that our clients, the Canadian taxpayers, are prepared to be generous with their tax dollars provided they see value for their money. When they perceive wasteful expenditures, or if they perceive a lack of controls, or when the Auditor General of this country tells them, as he did in 1976, that their parliamentarians have lost control or are about to lose control of the public purse, then the resistance of taxpayers to taxation is increased.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you seen this ad in today's Globe?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They take it upon themselves to exploit every conceivable tax loophole so as to frustrate what they call the insatiable appetite of wasteful big government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: $16,000 for this ad alone in today's Globe.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unfortunately, that perception of big wasteful government remains the perception of many of my con-stitutents and it is this same perception, I suggest, which

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
causes Canadians to call for greater government expenditure cuts.
As I shall demonstrate in a few moments, my responsibilities as President of the Treasury Board extend to a wide range of reforms in these areas in terms of the accountability and management of the public service. I have spoken at some length upon these matters in this House in the past. In a moment I shall describe some significant developments since my last report. All must be placed in the context of a firm commitment by this government to accountability and providing taxpayers with value for their money so that the perception which I referred to of wasteful expenditures which developed in the past will be eliminated. I am not asking for elimination of the perception simply on the basis of rhetoric and stated intentions, Mr. Speaker, but only on the basis of performance, which I believe we will be able to demonstrate to the satisfaction of parliamentarians and to the satisfaction of the public. We have not reached our destination, but we are well on the road.
Before I review with the House some of these initiatives and programs, I should like to refer to a specific request which is referred to in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, as described on page 27 of the document entitled "The Budget in More Detail."

More precisely, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has asked Treasury Board to cut by $100 million the government's annual administrative and general expenses. Mr. Speaker, that is indeed a challenge which I accept with enthusiasm and upon which we have already set our sights. Without overstressing the difficulties and the efforts required to reach that objective, Mr. Speaker, I commit myself not to stop at the $100 million mark should I find ways to save more without jeopardizing the services we are expected to offer to the public. I have already been asked where we shall apply the axe to make such savings. As I said in the past, Mr. Speaker, our policy is not to use an axe but rather a scalpel. What it means is that we will scrutinize specific fields where it is possible to make those savings. By way of example I would simply mention the fields of telecommunications, printing, photocopying, travel expenses and others. We have launched several studies and I am confident that, under the guidance of experts in the secretariat and the office of the Comptroller General, my colleagues in Treasury Board and I will be able to deliver the goods. [English]
I should like to refer to the progress which the government has been making in reforming the management of the Government of Canada in general. Hon. members will recall that on March 31, 1981, I tabled a progress report to Parliament entitled "Accountable Management". That document outlined the reforms which have been instituted by the government during the past four years and, in particular, set out the
government's response to the final report of the Lambert Royal Commission.
Today I am pleased to make a further progress report to the House. In doing so, I shall speak on behalf of my cabinet colleagues and on behalf of Treasury Board, which functions as the principal management area of government.
"Accountable Management" discussed government action in relation to the royal commission's recommendations and proposals under seven broad categories. In reporting on progress today, I shall follow those seven broad categories. They are as follows: The concept of a fiscal plan; second, a discipline on the resource allocation process related to the fiscal plan; third, accountability of government to Parliament; fourth, accountability within government; fifth, accountability and efficiency in the administration of financial systems; sixth, accountability and efficiency in human resource management; and seventh, a continuing strategy for reform.
[ Translation]
Honourable members will have noted that in last week's budget, my colleague, the Minister of Finance followed a practice started with last year's budget, namely the introduction in Parliament of a financial plan covering several years. As indicated in the document entitled "Accountable Management" which I just quoted, the 1980 financial plan covered four years instead of five, as was recommended by the Lambert Commission. But in 1981 we have a five-year plan. The publication of this financial plan therefore complies with the first of the two basic recommendations of the Lambert Commission, namely that the government project over several years its profits and expenditures for specific functions. That is a first and essential step towards ensuring parliamentary control over public expenditures and it is the basis upon which we can ensure responsible management within government.
The second basic recommendation of the Lambert Commission was to conduct an in-depth review of the definition and division of responsibilities in public administration so as to provide cabinet with the information it requires to limit public expenditures, and to ensure that departments and organizations follow sound management practices to provide taxpayers with adequate value for their tax dollars.
The policy and expenditure management system described in "Accountable Management" which is being applied for the second year, has an increasing influence on the procedures followed by government in establishing priorities, and arriving at necessary compromises between departments sharing the available resources, to ensure that programs are managed according to a results oriented approach.

Hon. members will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I recently sought their reaction to the new form of the estimates which has been developed by the Comptroller General. The government intends to proceed with this very important project. Not only will it provide Parliament with financial and program information in a more useful form, but it will also provide the
November 16, 1981

basis for results-oriented management of departmental programs.
The Comptroller General has also proceeded with improvements in systems for the management of financial resources. I shall refer to these systems in greater detail in a moment.
The Lambert report and the report of the Special Committee on Personnel Management and the Merit Principle, the D'Avignon report, both recommended a major realignment of the roles and responsibilities of the central agencies in the management of human resources and proposed a series of reforms in the personnel management function.
In addressing the roles of the central agencies, the government recognizes that the Public Service Commission derives its authority from the Public Service Employment Act while the Treasury Board's authority in the field of personnel management derives from the Financial Administration Act on one hand, and the Public Service Staff Relations Act on the other hand.
A comprehensive review of all aspects of the personnel function in the light of these statutory authorities has resulted in the text of a formal agreement between the Public Service Commission as an agency which is accountable directly to Parliament, and the Treasury Board on behalf of the government. This agreement reviews the whole field of personnel management and identifies those functions over which each agency has exclusive authority, those functions for which each agency has responsibilities which have been delegated from another agency, and finally, those functions for which both agencies have shared interests and responsibilities.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this represents a major advance in resolving the uncertainty on the relative roles in personnel management. This uncertainty has existed in the public service ever since present legislation was enacted. In the functions which are shared between the two agencies, it has been agreed that Treasury Board should have the lead role and that major policy statements should be issued solely in the name of the Treasury Board, with acknowledgement obviously where applicable, that the policy has been developed in consultation with the Public Service Commission. One very practical result of this is that there is to be a single Handbook for Managers on Personnel Management.
A further step is to thoroughly overhaul the personnel Management Manual of the Treasury Board and to incorporate the Staffing Manual of the Public Service Commission so that there will only be one personnel management manual in the public service. The Secretary of the Treasury Board and the Chairman of the Public Service Commission will be jointly communicating details of this agreement to all departments and to all agencies of the public service.
The agreement in question also covers the roles to be played by the central agencies and deputy heads in the administration of the new management category, the creation of which has now been completed. Of course, it is very important to ensure
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
that firm, co-ordinated leadership in career planning for this vital management resource is evident from the outset.
Also hon. members will recall that the Lambert and D'Avignon reports recommended that the whole staffing function be transferred from the Public Service Commission to the Treasury Board. The government is confident that such a drastic measure should not be contemplated at this time because it would cause a disruption for several years in a personnel system which is already heavily burdened by change. The government believes it will be far better to undertake further reforms in the personnel function on the basis of the substantial agreement on roles which has now been reached between the Treasury Board and the Public Service Commission.
In addition to this update on accountable management, I should like to report to hon. members on some activities of the Office of the Comptroller General. It is particularly important that I deal with the activities of the Comptroller General during the course of the budget debate because they are fundamental to achieving our primary objective on the expenditure side of fiscal policy; that is to say, value for money, value for our taxpayers' dollars.

To begin with, I should like to refer to IMPAC, which is short for "Improvement in Management Practices and Controls", a major initiative of the Comptroller General designed to make sure that departments conceive, implement and use sound management practices, in other words, to make sure that objectives are defined as clearly as possible, that activities are planned, that the ensuing activities are checked against those planned, and that the results obtained are assessed.
To be effective, the various steps of all sound management practices must be integrated. For instance, good control is based on sound planning and the setting of relevant objectives depends on a clear review of past experiences. From this definition, it is clear that this system is neither a new management theory nor a solution geared to special problems within the civil service, but rather a means of improving management permanently and economically. This approach requires close co-operation between the office of the Comptroller General and departmental managers in order to identify the shortcomings of management practices, conceive an integrated plan of action to correct the identified shortcomings, and implement the plan of action.

I want to stress the comprehensiveness of the IMPAC approach. In the past it would seem that concerted efforts to strengthen one element of good management tended to occur at the expense of neglecting others. Because IMPAC insists on the integrity of a department's management processes, it is essential to set priorities for improvement and to phase in the required action with a clear view of the whole context.
The scope and complexity of the IMPAC project are formidable. Let me give examples. First, at the moment IMPAC embraces the 31 largest departments and agencies of govern-

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
ment which together account for 85 per cent of total government expenditure, excluding debt payments, and 95 per cent of public service employees.
Second, the action plan of a typical department includes dozens of projects involving hundreds of person-months of effort and several million dollars, spread over three to five years.
Third, the action plan addresses problems which are inherently difficult to overcome, for instance, measuring performance in areas where the products are very hard to quantify, such as scientific research or policy formulation.
Another problem is the sheer size and diversity of the operations of many departments. This poses technical obstacles to the installation of management reporting systems in order to meet the information needs of various levels of management without becoming impossibly complicated.
Fourth, and perhaps more importantly, implementing 1MPAC depends on changing attitudes and work habits, a process which never occurs easily or quickly.
Finally, comprehensive management improvement requires a sustained act of vision and will. In the dynamic environment of the public service, with frequently changing priorities and personnel, it is challenging to keep a long-term initiative of this importance focused on the real problems of individual departments.
Bearing in mind the nature of IMPAC which I have just described, let me quickly review for the benefit of hon. members of the House what has actually been accomplished in the three years since the Comptroller General launched this initiative. First, there have been surveys of all but two of the 31 departments included in the IMPAC study. They were completed in the spring of 1980. The thirtieth was completed this spring, and the thirty-first is now underway. As I described earlier, comprehensive action plans now exist for 25 departments. They have been endorsed by the Office of the Comptroller General; six more are expected over the next couple of months.
Implementation progress varies widely among departments, as some might expect. In some we are beginning to see much improved management practices. For example, in the Department of Public Works, this means setting up the systems needed to implement revenue dependency which, as hon. members are aware, cabinet approved in principle earlier this year. For the Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission, this means action to reduce over and underpayments of unemployment insurance benefits.
In the few moments which remain I should like to refer to some of the other initiatives. Program evaluation is absolutely fundamental to good, solid management practices. This is well established. Quite recently I issued a guide to program evaluation which was distributed to parliamentarians. Time does not permit me to devote the time to program evaluation that I would like. The same is true of internal audit. It is well advanced, but again the time remaining does not permit me to give hon. members of the House the benefit of a full report on
the status of internal audit. I can assure the House that, in keeping with the recommendations which have come forth from the Auditor General and the Lambert commission over the years, we are well advanced.
I have already referred to the reform of the estimates. Of course, Members of Parliament have concrete evidence of that reform through the projects tabled in the House and distributed by me to all members. What all these initiatives have in common is strengthened accountability. Particularly in times of economic hardship governments must set an example by finding ways to do more with less.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When will you start?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The initiatives I have described today are providing Parliament and the government with the tools needed to do that job.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Convince the taxpayer of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In conclusion, the fiscal management of Canada is moving ahead on all fronts.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You cannot even keep a straight face when you say that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Indeed it is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like a little order, Mr. Speaker. I hope hon. members would like to be educated on the reforms which are taking place. Fiscal management is moving ahead efficiently, creatively, responsibly and, above all, is responsive to the needs of Canadians. My colleagues and I congratulate the Minister of Finance for responding so directly to the plight of those Canadians who are suffering from high interest rates, for the thrust of restraint and deficit reduction, and for the very creative steps toward long overdue tax reform.
On the expenditure, management and accountability side, I am sure that my remarks today on the status of our ambitious government-wide reforms on financial accountability, personnel management and management practices will satisfy members that this government is well on the road to obtaining more value for the taxpayer's dollars.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to take part in this budget debate. I regret the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), but I understand that he is unavoidably absent today.

I regret it in particular because I find it almost impossible to address the budget without some reference to its author, since,
November 16, 1981

unfortunately, I think one of the major deficiencies in the budget reflects the approach that has been taken to this House and to the question of the economy by the Minister of Finance.
What we are dealing with here, Mr. Speaker, is probably the most dishonest budget ever introduced in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has deliberately cultivated a reputation as a man of cunning, a man who will never give us a straight answer. I think we on this side of the House have to say that has served him well as a minister who did not want to answer questions but, sir, a different standard is expected of a Minister of Finance; that is, a standard of honesty.
The millions of individuals whose private economic decisions make our economy falter or make our economy grow must be able to trust the word of the chief economic spokesman of government. It his word cannot be trusted, then they will delay their economic decisions, whether those are individual decisions to get new training, to seek to buy a new house, to start a business or to make major investment decisions about whether to invest in Canada or elsewhere, whether to start a megaproject or delay it. Sir, where there is no trust there is no economic progress.
While this project has done immense immediate harm to hundreds of thousands of individual Canadians, while it has done harm that is literally irreparable to many of our fellow citizens-many of the people affected by this budget will never get over its impact upon their lives-the deepest damage it does is the damage to Canada's future.
We have become accustomed to Liberal budgets which have failed to build on the creative capacities of our people or our country, and that is bad enough. What is worse about this budget is that it is so tricky, so untrustworthy, so dishonest as to make it impossible for anyone to believe the word or count on the future actions of the Minister of Finance or a government which makes him its principal economic spokesman.
That is not simply the opinion expressed by members of this House; that is the opinion of the stock market. The stock market has already registered its official response. It fell 39 points after the budget came down and now, after investors have had an opportunity to consider the impact of the budget over the weekend, it has fallen another 32 points. That is after people have read the fine print in the budget.
We know that across the country and, indeed, across the world people are sitting down this very day and reading that budget. They are reading the fine print and trying to decide whether to cancel or carry on activities which would have created jobs and growth and which might have created confidence and progress in Canada.
Some of the early decisions have been taken already, in the immediate aftermath of the budget. It is difficult to get current reports on the response to a budget which came down only on Thursday. Naturally, some of those responses have
The Budget-Mr. Clark
been in the housing Field first, the field where there is real urgency to get on with development and construction.
I regret to report to the House that in Winnipeg Mar-West has stopped plans for a 1,500 unit apartment development because of the Liberal budget brought down on Thursday night. In Vancouver, Inter-West has stopped plans for a total of 605 duplex and apartment units because of the budget brought down on Thursday night by the Liberal government. Again in Vancouver, Community Buildings has stopped a total of 261 duplex and apartment units because of the budget brought down by the Liberal government last Thursday night. A total of 460 units in London, Ontario, and 350 in St. John's, Newfoundland have been stopped because of the budget brought down by the Liberal government on Thursday night. In total, in one day the Liberal budget brought down by the Minister of Finance has caused over 3,000 units of housing to be cancelled in this country. Those were units of housing under construction before the budget was brought down; they were under construction even at a time when it was risky to engage in that kind of enterprise. Now, as its latest contribution to the housing crisis in this country, the Liberal government has brought in a budget that has caused 3,000 units that were under construction to be withdrawn from the market available to Canadians.
That is the First wave of decision, Mr. Speaker-a reversal of plans to develop things, to build things, to make this country go. That is the first wave of plans that have been changed as the result of this budget.
Other decisions like that are going to come about; that is as certain as anything we know in this House. In some cases decisions will be reversed because programs that Liberal governments introduced as incentives have been abruptly cut off; in other cases because individuals or enterprises will simply decide that they cannot invest in a country whose government they cannot trust.
As we in this House know, the trustworthiness of this government is already in tatters as a result of its breaking its word on wage and price controls and because it opposed an 18 cents per gallon increase in the price of gasoline and then introduced a 65 cents per gallon increase in the price of gasoline.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This budget carries deceit a step further. It quite deliberately tries to fool the people of Canada about the basic purposes and impact of the budget.
Let me contrast some of the minister's claims with the truth, Mr. Speaker. He says that the purpose of his tax changes is to "improve the fairness and equity of the system." The truth is that he is providing no new tax credits for those low-income Canadians who pay little or no tax. He is cutting the tax rates only at the top income levels. He is raising taxes for all single workers who earn in excess of $17,000, including the heads of single parent families, and he has smuggled in a bundle of new taxes that hit hardest at the ordinary working man and woman in this country.

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Clark
He claims that this is a budget of restraint. The truth is that government spending will increase by 22 per cent, that this budget sucks into the federal treasury the highest percentage of annual income since 1946, the first year of reconstruction, and increases government spending on virtually every item except health and post-secondary education.
The minister says that the main thrust of the budget is to fight inflation. The truth is that he plans to collect $4.2 billion more in energy taxes next year, virtually all of which will be inflationary, and his new taxes on employee benefits will guarantee new inflationary wage demands.
He says he has a plan for economic development in the 1980s. The truth is that his plan is just another promise of a couple of studies, a new bureaucracy and a vague commitment to consultation that, at best, will take us back to the sectoral studies of 1977-78, while job destruction proceeds apace in Canada and the megaprojects remain on the drawing boards.
He told the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements that he intended to cut his obligation to the provinces by only $1.5 billion in transfer payments for health, post-secondary education, social assistance and social services in 1982-83 and 1983-84. The truth is that he was preparing to cut that obligation by $1.9 billion during that period and a further $3.8 billion during the next three years.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) shakes his head, and I can understand why he would shake his head. Canadians across this country are shaking their heads at the deceit of this Liberal budget and the degree to which they have been betrayed by a government which not only had an obligation, but which had also given undertakings to come to the aid of Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Again, the Minister of Finance says that since 1973 Canada has been second only to Japan in terms of real growth. The truth is that between 1975 and 1980 we have ranked next to last in growth, despite the fact that we supply a larger share of our own oil needs than any of the six nations with which we are compared. Those are some of the differences between the minister's claims and the truth.
Perhaps the best way to judge this budget which masquerades as tax reform and as help for the ordinary Canadian is to look at exactly who is helped and who is hurt by this budget. The list of those who benefit is very short. The ranks of those who suffer include almost every Canadian.
To start, let us look at who this budget helps. First of all, and most of all, it helps the treasury of the federal government. From March 1, 1981, to March 1, 1983, the federal government will receive-I want hon. members to note this figure-$27.5 billion more on a national accounts basis. There will be an increase in its revenues of 52 per cent over two fiscal years. Therefore, the federal government is the big winner while individual Canadians lose their homes, their businesses,
their farms and their hopes. While provinces are forced to cut back on schooling and health care, the federal government is looking after itself, taking money from the people of Canada, raising Ottawa's revenues by 52 per cent over two fiscal years.
Who else benefits? The rich who are on salary benefit. This budget proposes cuts in marginal tax rates for people with high incomes. Therefore, wealthy individuals who get most of their income from salaries will benefit from this budget. The general rule is that Canadians who earn salaries over $40,000 a year are likely to gain from this budget. They are the people who are helped, particularly if their salaries are their principal sources of income. Who else does it help? It helps deputy ministers, indeed. Deputy ministers are among the principal beneficiaries of this particular budget because they are in the category of people who are paid very well and who draw most of their income from salaries. Those are the people who benefit from the budget that was brought down by the Minister of Finance on Thursday. Almost everyone else in the country suffers.
Again, one group which is helped by the budget is the banks and other lending institutions which hold mortgages. They will be directly helped by this budget because they will get the guarantee on the mortgage renewal loans they extend to those home owners whom the government decides happen to be in dire straits. There is another small group which will be helped. It will consist of the new bureaucrats who are hired to decide just who among those home owners, farmers and small-business men in dire straits is eligible for the meagre relief the budget provides. That, by the way, is the only job-creation component I can find in this new budget. It proposes to set up a new group of bureaucrats to decide who in Canada is really in trouble and then distribute meagre pittances of money to those Canadians.
The final category of people who will be helped by this budget consists of the government's old friends, the tax accountants and the tax lawyers. They will do not quite as well as the federal government will, but they will benefit from a budget which causes most Canadians to suffer.
That is the little list, the very short list of people who will benefit from this budget which was brought down in the name of equity. It is an odd kind of equity when the highest paid public servant in Canada receives a tax cut of at least $700 a year while Canadians who are too poor to pay tax get no help at all.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Shame, shame!
[ Translation]
The other thing for us to do now is to identify the victims. Who are they? First, the Canadians who will lose their job or who will not be hired because the budget does nothing to correct the current recession which is stifling the labour market. The main victims of the loss of job opportunities are young Canadians, people in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec and factory workers. These Canadians are penalized by this Liberal budget. Other victims include every Canadian family
November 16, 1981

that uses heating oil and drives a car. At the end of 1982 they will each have paid at least $900 in indirect taxes to the federal government since the last budget. Also, low income Canadians who have to bear an excessive tax burden are penalized by this Liberal budget, as well as renters who are facing a housing shortage with a potential black market in many urban areas of tremendous rent increases. Because of these increases, the budget discourages rather than promotes the building of rental housing in spite of a shortfall in rental unit construction in the last few years. Canadian renters will be penalized by this Liberal budget. Because the basic tax rate is reduced to $200, every single person in Canada, including single parents, with an income of over $17,000 a year will have to pay more taxes. No assistance will be offered to single people who make under $17,000. Moreover, energy costs for both groups will increase tremendously without any compensation being offered. These Canadians will be penalized by the Liberal budget. In addition, the average worker will see his real income decrease next year. For the fifth year in a row, this Canadian citizen will be penalized by a Liberal budget. [English]
I want to speak for a moment about the provision as it affects employee benefits, because I think nothing better demonstrates the lack of equity in this fraud of a budget which has the effrontery to call itself a budget of equity. The minister spoke with some passion about closing the loopholes in the tax system. I think it worth noting in passing that what are called loopholes today by a Liberal government were called incentives yesterday by a Liberal government when they were introduced by that party.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

will now have to pay a new Liberal tax on those employee benefits. Every salesman or saleswoman whose company provides a company automobile will now have to pay a new Liberal tax on that company car. Every worker-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Liberal party thinks it is just fine. We hear a great deal of heckling from the minister of state responsible from time to time for finance and from the government side. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are not finished with the list of people who are affected by this new Liberal tax on employee benefits. The language of the law is not quite clear in the documents brought down. We will have to wait and see what it is as we get into more debate, but it occurred to me on the basis of what is available in the documents now that every worker whose employer maintains a daycare facility may now be forced to pay a new Liberal tax on daycare in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It also appears that every worker who is let go from his or her job may now have to pay a new Liberal tax on severance pay as a result of the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance last Thursday night. Those are some of the people who will have to pay.

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Clark
There are other victims of this budget brought down last Thursday night. There are the small business proprietors who used the Small Business Development Bond to get capital below market rates to expand their enterprises and provide new jobs in Canada. They will now be able to get capital only if their businesses are about to go into bankruptcy. It is no longer a development bond, it is now a small-business survival bond, and a group of bureaucrats, the only new people hired by this government, are going to decide who gets to survive in the small-business community and who is forced by Liberal economic policy to go under.
Among the others who suffer from this budget are the poor who pay no income tax. They will obtain no new benefits from this budget while the burden of indirect energy taxes will continue to rise and health services may deteriorate because of the reductions in established programs financing. Those low-income Canadians across the country are going to be hurt by the budget that was brought down and they will be hurt directly.
Again, the reductions in the established programs financing will also increase pressures for lay-offs at hospitals and postsecondary institutions across the country. People whose jobs are in jeopardy because of this budget brought down on Thursday night are among those who will suffer.
Young people who will not be able to find a job may not be able to attend community colleges or universities because the established programs funding reduction may result in higher tuition fees or in a shutdown of departments or programs in institutions close to where they would attend. Those young Canadians are in need of training so they can help build our future. Those young Canadians will suffer and be hurt because of the budget brought down by this Liberal government last Thursday night.
Farmers will see the energy portion of their costs go up while commodity prices fall and the grossly inadequate financial assistance provided by the budget is available only after farmers are in "financial distress". Therefore, most of the farmers in Canada will suffer as a result of the budget that was brought down.
Home owners who lost their homes or were forced to renew mortgages before September 1 at rates which sharply reduced their standard of living will get no help at all from this government. They, too, are people hurt by the budget that was brought down last Thursday night, despite all of the empty promises made by the minister responsible for housing. Of the 920,000 households renewing mortgages after the cut-off date at sharply higher rates, less than 2 per cent will get any help and they will have to take on additional debt burdens before they get that help.
Let me deal with the most cruel deceit of all in this deceitful budget, namely the minister's claim that it helps those Canadians who are suffering directly from the impact of this government's own high interest rate policy. I think it important that every Canadian home owner, every Canadian small-business man and every Canadian farmer know exactly what this government is doing to them by this budget which increases so
dramatically the revenues of the federal government and increases so dramatically the hardship of the ordinary, average Canadian.
Every member of this House knows the dimension of the crisis facing Canadian home owners. We on this side of the House have been raising the matter day after day through questions, through petitions and through demands for action from the government. More than 900,000 of our fellow Canadian citizens are facing mortgage renewal within the next 12 months, a period during which, by the minister responsible for housing's own figures, interest rates will remain at or near their present punitive levels. Even the minister responsible for housing, who by now should be the resigned minister responsible for housing, admits in his own department's documents the following:
-mortgage interest rates have now reached the point where it cannot be argued that the incidence of hardship of renewal is minimal.
It cannot be argued that that hardship is minimal. That is the minister's own statement. There are 900,000 Canadians facing what the minister admits is more than minimal hardship. And what does the government offer? By its own figures, it proposes programs that at the maximum will affect some 12,500 families.
We have heard a great deal about dire straits, Mr. Speaker. As I travelled across the country through community after community, people kept telling me that their community's name had been changed to "dire straits". The people from Kelowna came to me and told me that Kelowna is an old Indian word for "dire straits". We may not know exactly where "dire straits" is, but we now know the population. The population of "dire straits" is 12,500 people, and that is all. That is the only group of Canadians in danger of losing their homes which this government proposes to help.
At most, one out of every 75 Canadians facing mortgage renewals at these astronomical rates will get any help from this government. One out of 75 is barely a third of the almost 40,000 Canadians which the minister responsible for housing, again in his own documents, admits already have to pay well over 30 per cent of their family income in mortgage payments. Again, if I might, let me quote what the minister said in speaking about these people. He said:
Their choices are to pay a very large proportion of their income to retain their house, try to sell their home or just walk away and face foreclosures.
This government has sealed the choice for two out of every three of those Canadians. Those Canadians can either sell or walk away from their homes.
But what about that minority which the government says it is going to help meet soaring mortgage costs? For most of them the government, in fact, is providing no help at all. It is saying to them: "You go deeper and longer in debt by adding additional interest costs to your mortgage, and if you then find you cannot carry that kind of debt load, we will bail out the lender." That is exactly what the so-called guarantee program is about. It is not a home assistance program at all; the government has brought in a bank protection plan.
November 16, 1981

We have all heard the Minister of Finance during the past couple of weeks waging his phoney war of words against the banks. Then he brought in his budget, the budget in which he could have done something about the banks he was criticizing if he had been serious. He did do something; he protected the banks while sentencing thousands of Canadians to the almost certain loss of their homes.
I have just been handed a note, Mr. Speaker, which states that the stock market has gone down today by some 50 points. That is a total drop of 86 points since the MacEachen budget was brought in. That gives us an indication of what the budget has done to the confidence of those people in Canada whose confidence is essential if we are to continue to grow, to provide jobs and to realize the potential of this country.

And now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the situation of renters. Let us see how the government is helping tenants, a group that will become even larger when thousands more Canadians will be obliged to leave their homes and move to apartments. In his own documents the minister responsible for housing says that 105,000 Canadians are obliged to spend more than 30 per cent of their disposable income on housing. One reason is the housing shortage that exists in practically all Canadian cities. According to the government's figures, vacancy rates are at their lowest levels in five years. The government's response is to provide loans for exactly 15,000 new rental units next year. This does not even cover the requirements of our major cities. What about requirements throughout the country? As a result of these loans, the average rent for these units will be about $600 per month. To make matters worse, it seems the Minister of Finance is taking away the MURB program with the other hand. The result will be a reduction in the amount of capital available for the construction of new rental units, far beyond the 15,000 units being offered.
Because of this government and this liberal budget, not more but fewer new rental units will be built next year. It is not exaggeration to say that because of these liberal policies, the very existence of the housing industry in Canada could be threatened. This is a budget that is leaving hundreds of thousands of Canadians in a truly desperate situation. To all Canadians on low or fixed incomes, who are faced with massive increases in energy and housing costs, the budget does not offer a penny's worth of assistance. For all Canadians to whom the Minister responsible for housing said to wait until the budget was brought down before deciding what to do with their homes, the message is now very clear. As the minister said so succinctly: Sell or drop the whole thing. To all small-business men and to farmers whose way of life is being threatened, the budget says: Sink or swim, we are not going to help you.
The Budget-Mr. Clark

For small-business men and farmers on the verge of bankruptcy as a result of this government's high interest rate policy, the story in this budget is sadly the same. The minister pretends to hold out a helping hand. That helping hand, it turns out, doubles into a fist to sock them in the face. The minister pretends to extend the Small Business Development Bond program to unincorporated businesses and farmers. In fact, he has gutted that entire program and virtually cancelled it. He now limits access to the program to those small businesses and farmers which the minister describes as being "in financial difficulty". It is no longer a development program at all. There is no longer access to that program for any farmer or small-business man who is in a position to develop or expand his operation. Access to that program is now available only to those who are bleeding to death financially. It is just the kind of business you would expect the banks to make even subsidized loans to. What this budget offers them is not a development program but a band-aid so that they can go on bleeding. For a measurement of the effectiveness of this program you have only to look at the government's estimate that it will cost the treasury only $20 million in the next two years compared with $200 million now. That means the government anticipates approximately one tenth as many loans under this program as there has been to date.
The impact on agriculture is as severe. There has been a proposal to increase the funding of the Farm Credit Corporation to about one tenth of the amount that our party proposed. We have done a quick calculation as to how many farmers will benefit from those Farm Credit Corporation lending arrangements. How many farmers will benefit by aid and money from the Farm Credit Corporation? The total number of farmers across the country who could benefit from Farm Credit Cor-portion aid is 225.
The small business development bond, with its strict limitation of aid to people who are already almost out of business and on the verge of bankruptcy, will benefit a pittance of perhaps 350 farmers. That means to the Canadian farming population, to people who keep this a food-producing nation and who have borne the cost and difficulty of trying to compete in inflationary times longer than most of us, that this government, whose green-hatted minister spoke through that green hat so eloquently about help that would be available to them, proposes to extend help to exactly 575 farmers across the country and the rest can go broke.
In addition, farmers could be among those Canadians who will be severely affected by changes in the averaging provisions brought in by this government. Farmers and others respond to incentive in a country like Canada, and do not seek out loopholes.
The minister spoke fiercely of closing loopholes. He spoke about it with all the rhetoric of someone embarking on another crusade. He forgot to mention that most of what he called loopholes were written into Canadian tax law by governments of which he was a member. Those governments called them incentives at that time.

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Clark
I will not read these into the record today but I have available quotes from the Hon. Edgar Benson, Donald Macdonald and John Turner when they introduced these very loopholes the Minister of Finance is today crusading against. When these architects of Canadian tax loopholes introduced them, they were not called loopholes. They introduced them because they believed they would help Canadians go out and invest in the country, take risks, create jobs and make the country grow.
This House of Commons will have to scrutinize very carefully just what the effect of this part of the budget will be. It is my suspicion that it was designed by people who have an admirable zeal against abuse but an abysmal understanding of how these incentives are used by ordinary Canadians to make the Canadian economy grow and create jobs and opportunites for citizens across our country.
One example of this is the change in the capital cost allowance. This will yield the government, according to its own figures, almost $1 billion in new revenue. When the Hon. John Turner introduced that proposal, of which he was the architect, it was to stimulate Canadian jobs in the Canadian manufacturing industry and to help smaller enterprises across the country get on with the work of making Canada grow.
We know this change in the capital cost allowance will bring a billion dollars to the government in the first year, but we do not know what damage it will do to the economy. Before this Parliament approves the disintegration of that incentive we will want to know what damage it does to the Canadian economy and not just simply the richness it adds to the already fat federal treasury. Other members will want to pursue this question. I simply want to remind the House again that what the government now calls loopholes were very recently called incentives.
This budget hits dental plans and health plans in Canada and it may well hit daycare. It hits incentive to businesses which want to expand in this country. This budget, in the name of the crusade against incentive, may very well cut deeply into the capacity of the nation to grow.
Not only are health and dental plans affected, but this budget seeks to destroy employee share purchase and profitsharing plans. It seeks to destroy them and undercuts them. What is the logic that causes the government to take a position in the budget against employee share purchase plans and employee profit-sharing plans? It makes it more difficult for Canadians with no pension plans to put money into retirement programs like RRSPs. Why? What is the logic of that in a society like ours? Even for this government of so-called economic nationalists it reduces the incentives for Canadians to invest in Canadian equities. It ends special allowances, at the end of next year, for those Canadians willing to work to develop our north. It makes every Canadian immigrant a second-class citizen when it comes to providing financial help to his or her family. As I indicated, it comes down hard on company automobiles used by all those "rich" Canadians like salesmen and local managers.
