subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance was on the television program "Question Period", and he was asked whether we are in a recession. He used a rather technical argument about not having two quarters together to indicate we are not in a recession yet, but he gave everyone to understand that he is working on it just as hard as he can and that he will have us there very quickly. Indeed, this is a recession budget. This is a document which not only pulls the economy down but also pulls down the state of enthusiasm of Canadians about our potential in this country. That is the stark reality of this budget. It was produced at a time when virtually every economic indicator available to the minister-growth rates, unemployment rates, the CPI, inventory and export figures, consumer confidence measurements-told him that our economy already was sliding into serious recession. Even his position of a year ago to do nothing and hope that the Americans would pull us out was no longer sustainable. His own documents forecast poor economic performance south of the border; yet, facing all that evidence, the minister offered nothing at all to make things better and a great deal to make things worse. Canadians are entitled to believe that this minister's real policy is that there is nothing like a good depression to correct economic problems.
As bad as the economic implications of this document might be, in some respects it is even more depressing for what it does to the deep and essential values of our society. Those of us on this side of the House and, I believe, the vast majority of Canadians believe that the ultimate strength of our nation lies in its people and in the energy and enterprise they bring to building their lives and, by building their lives, helping to build the country. Most Canadians live with a faith in individual responsibility and initiative, and they hope that if they are responsible and innovative in their own lives, they will be encouraged and even rewarded for their effort.
This depressing budget offers neither encouragement nor reward. Its only winner is a government which continues to claim more and more for itself. What is so shocking about this is that its message to the people of Canada is almost: "Why bother?" Why should individuals bother? For a young couple, why bother to scrimp and save for a home of their own? This government does not care if they keep or lose that home. If you are a small-business man or a farmer, why bother to put your life savings, your work and your dreams on the line? This government has no real commitment to you. If you are an entrepreneur who wants to build something for yourself and your country, why bother? This government has no direction to offer and no vision of a country in which you can join and be a part.
November 16, 1981

All those values which have built this country in the past, and in which many Canadians still believe, are shut out of this budget and in many cases are cut off by this budget. [Translation]
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address my comments to the backbenchers on the government side. They have a crucial role to play. We on the opposition side can fight the budget and we will do so with all the means at our disposal. However, only the Liberal backbenchers can prevail upon the Minister of Finance to do the only reasonable thing, which is to withdraw this document and substitute for it a budget that is worthy of Canada. I am not speaking glibly in putting this challenge to the members on the opposite side. I am challenging them because, on a matter as important as the constitution, some of these members said they were prepared to defend a principle in which they truly believe. I now say to them that this budget must be changed because of the harm it is doing to Canadians.
I know that many members on the opposite side are aware of the plight of the people we are representing here. They know because they can see what is happening in their own ridings, what Canadians who are trying to hold onto their homes, farms and businesses are going through. They know that Canadians with low incomes and pensions are in great difficulty, and that it will get even worse when they try to cope with rising energy costs and other price increases. They know, because people tell them and because they can see for themselves that Canada urgently needs an economic policy that will help people to get organized and to know where they are going. The government members know perfectly well that none of this is offered in the budget. If they want to join forces with us, with our party and with the party on my left, we can force the minister to change his budget. For Canada's sake, I ask them to join us in this request.

In his remarks on Thursday night the minister as much as confessed that for the last 18 months this government has been preoccupied with the Constitution and with the question of energy. He intimated, in his view at least, that those problems were over for Canada. In so far as the Constitution is concerned, we certainly hope it will be possible to find a way to resolve that question, and we hope the government will consider realistically some of the impacts its policies are having on energy policy in the country. The minister intimated that for him at least that preoccupation was passed, and he raised our hopes that there might now be a willingness on the part of this government to address the question which the great majority of Canadians believes is the principal question before the country, and that is the question of the Canadian economy, how we can get it growing again, how we can stop Canadians from experiencing personal disaster and how we can stop the country from experiencing national disaster.
In presenting his budget last Thursday night the Minister of Finance had a rare opportunity to provide some leadership to
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
the country. As a result of the energy agreement-the details of which are obviously controversial-the Government of Canada will have massive new revenues of about $55 billion over the next five years. Those revenues would be sufficient to reduce the deficit and provide real aid to those Canadians in need and to build in or maintain incentive to the private sector, which has always been the engine of growth in this country and will continue to be the engine of growth, unless this budget drives entrepreneurs away or drives the entrepreneurial spirit away from those who remain in the country.
Instead of that response to the great opportunity for leadership, what we got was an attempt to fool Canadians. We got a budget which was a trick. It was a dishonest document designed to pretend that there was action and designed to pretend there was reform. But it was in fact a budget which will impose an unbearably hard burden upon countless average Canadians and has as its principal purpose the enrichment of the federal government. This budget sells our country short. We need in Canada now incentive to investment so that those Canadians who want to go out and take risks and make the nation grow will have the encouragement of their government to do so rather than being stopped by that government from doing so.
In a country like ours, the future of which lies in a competitive edge in the world, we desperately need much more investment in research and development. We need help for Canadians who want to go out and find job retraining so that they will have skills which suit the new decade that is developing. We need policies to encourage export promotion. We need policies to encourage the productive side of a country which has always been immensely productive when its government encouraged its people to take advantage of the resources that are here. However, what we need most of all is a sense that the government is facing our economic situation honestly and dealing with it seriously. We have none of that in this budget. It is a document that is inaccurate; it is a document that is inadequate; it is a document that is dishonest; it is a document which should be either withdrawn or changed fundamentally.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are here at 4.30 in the afternoon on the second day of the budget debate. We just listened to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark). There are in Canada more than a million unemployed, inflation is running at about 13 per cent, farmers are losing their farms, the stock market is dropping rapidly. And where is the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)? Where is the cabinet?
Today during question period, I repeat the second day of the budget debate, when members of both opposition parties ought to have had an opportunity to question the Minister of Finance, where was he? Where is he now for this debate? I will tell you. He is five minutes from the House of Commons. He was there at the noon hour. He is having a private briefing with a limited number of reporters instead of being here in the

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
House of Commons to answer questions on the budget and listen to important speeches on this side of this House. Nothing can illustrate the arrogance and indifference to the people of Canada better than the absence of the minister from this crucial part of the debate this afternoon.
Having said that and having heard the budget last Thursday night, in terms of its content, in one sense at least I can understand why the minister is not here. Except for the 45,000 Canadian taxpayers who earn more than $100,000 a year and who will save $5,000 as a result of this budget, this budget is one without help, without heart and without hope for the people of Canada. To put it simply and accurately, as I shall try to develop in my comments this afternoon, this budget guarantees that Canada will not only have a severe but also a prolonged recession in the coming years.

In recent months the unemployed, wage earners, renters, home owners, young and middle-aged, had been hoping that their government would take measures to lighten their burden. But this government is bankrupt of ideas. It operates in a complete vacuum. They blame everybody else except themselves, of course. It is the fault of the Americans, the international situation, the angels and so forth. Everybody is responsible except the Liberals. And yet, other countries have succeeded in setting up original programs which have already paid off. I am thinking of France, for instance. That country does not have the same resources as we do, not by a long shot. And yet, it innovates by adopting grant programs and tax credit legislation for small and medium-sized businesses hiring youth; the state is thus creating jobs for young people. The French model is not necessarily fully compatible with the Canadian situation, but it does show that, through imagination and hard work, it is possible to get out of an economic stalemate.

Consider the problems and then think of the budget in the context of those very real human problems. First, the standard of living. For the past four years, Canadians have seen wages and salaries lag behind price increases. According to this budget, we are going to have a fifth year in a row of the same experience, a record sequence of years since World War II in which the standard of living of Canadians is going to decline.
Consider unemployment. For over three years, more than a million in real numbers, men and women of all ages who have wanted to work, have been unable to find a job. According to this budget, that situation is going not only to continue in 1982, but will get worse in 1983 and still worse in 1984. The most optimistic forecast found in the budget is that by 1985 we might finally begin to see a decline in the unemployment levels.
I want to stress that this budget is cause for despair, not simply for the unemployed men and women. It is also a matter of despair for all those men and women who are currently employed who feel quite insecure because of the economic
forecasts that are in the budget. They may have a job today, but they are appropriately apprehensive that they may lose it tomorrow.
In addition to the people who have lost their jobs or those who think they may, there are the parents of young men and women who this year are about to finish high school or a post-secondary education of some kind and will be looking for jobs. Those parents are very insecure about the prospect of their children being able to get a job in the coming year.
The concern, the insecurity, the despair is real in Canada. As leader of the New Democratic Party, it is entirely justified, I regret to say. One need only read the budget with some care to find that. There is not a single job-creation program in the budget for all of those people who are concerned.
The point is that our Minister of Finance thinks, and I use that term loosely, that Canada needs a recession to beat inflation. He is determined to inflict that recession upon us. He is going to sacrifice the production of goods and services that would be helpful in bringing down the level of prices if products were bring produced as well as provide jobs. He is also sacrificing the dignity that comes from work which is possessed by men and women who have a chance to contribute to the wellbeing of other people in society by their labour.
Quite apart from the lack of economic activity and the effects on human dignity with the perpetuation of this planned unemployment, which is what it is, I want to emphasize in my speech, and suggest some solution to it, that this approach is wrong economically. One might, under very peculiar and regrettable circumstances, allow for the kind of situation I have just described if it were necessary and if it were going to produce beneficial results down the road. I want to argue today that it is a profoundly wrong economic approach.
I would have hoped that after two years of this policy of high inflation rates related directly to high interest rates it would have been sufficient for the Minister of Finance in preparing this budget to come to his senses and change direction. I would have hoped he could have seen what Margaret Thatcher, by pursuing the same policies in England for three years, has inflicted upon the people of Great Britain. I would have hoped that he could see day after day what these policies under President Reagan are doing in the United States, and even that radical journal the Wall Street Journal has called into question recently the financial appropriateness of this approach to the economy.
Imbedded in the heart of the budget is this economic approach that is dependent on high interest rates that leaves unstated, but is there nonetheless, that if American interest rates increase, as a number of the long range forecasters are predicting, as surely as night follows day the Government of Canada, the Liberal government, will allow interest rates in Canada to continue to increase.
Whatever happened in the United Kingdom, United States and, importantly, whatever has happened in Canada as a result of this high interest rate policy has had no bearing on the arid,
November 16, 1981

academic, intellectual approach that is an arid, intellectual approach devoid of thought. It is an approach devoid of actually looking at the experience of what has happened in other countries.
Consider the impact of high interest rates on farmers. I talked to some farmers a short time ago in Saskatchewan. They told me directly how this interest rate policy affects them. Again, I should like to stress that I am not talking about the human impact. That is a fundamental concern because the Liberals like to boast that they are the pragmatic realists, that they are the competent managers of the economy.
I should like to deal with that issue in their terms. I asked the farmers, "Tell me directly what is happening with high interest rates in terms of its impact on you, as an economic unit, if you like." I received the following elementary points that should be of concern to the government. First, they said: "If we have to buy our machinery, whether it is made in Canada or imported from abroad, the high interest rate situation, the carrying charge that we have to pay, is just as bad". Their costs of production rise. Or they said to me: "If we have to carry inventories over the winter", which they do, "we have to pay 20 per cent plus." That also increases their production costs.
More often than not, the farmers of Canada are unable, for a variety of reasons, to pass their cost increases on to the consumers. They have to absorb them directly themselves and, therefore, the farmers' families suffer. But where a farmer can pass the increase on, and no one will blame him for it, the result is higher food prices for Canadian consumers. That is the result of high interest rates for the farming sector.
What has the government done? It has not changed the interest rate policy, and I will return to this point in a minute. It has pretended it is providing a solution for the farmers in difficulty. What is it, Mr. Speaker? In the budget the government will lend an additional $50 million at moderate interest to farmers who are on the brink of bankruptcy; but the Farm Credit Corporation's total lending budget will now represent nearly 2.6 per cent of the debts that Canada's farmers now owe. There will be no way for new farmers to expand or purchase needed equipment. There simply will not be enough money to keep more farmers from bankruptcy. That is the reality of the kind of assistance that the Liberal Party is prepared to provide for our farmers in difficulty.
Again from the point of view of economics alone, consider the small businesses. Before Parliament resumed, I was in Newfoundland where I visited Corner Brook and St. John's and, more particularly, the small community of Baie Verte. I should like to suggest this afternoon that Baie Verte is a microcosm of everything that is happening to the Canadian economy. In that community there are two mines that will close down. This is directly related to the interest rate factor.
The week before I visited Baie Verte I heard that one of the mines was to close because the markets in western Europe experienced a temporary turndown. Under normal circumstances, a mine or any other business can carry its inventory over a period of time until business picks up. It is particularly
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
interesting for this mine because it had increased its productivity by some 50 per cent in the past three years. It had invested new capital in the mine so that it would become more efficient. The ore body was good. However, the markets were down and it was paying, if I recall correctly-I know this is the framework of the loan, anyway-some 25 per cent to the banks. Its line of credit ran out. The banks shut the mine down. Several hundred employees were laid off as a result of high interest rates. These people were laid off from an efficient mine that could have continued to employ people and that could have realized a profit for the owners if a situation existed where there were normal interest rates and had the owners been able to survive another few months.
Approximately two miles up the road was another mine. The day I arrived I heard that it was to shut down. I think it is due to be shut down by Christmas. This mine illustrates a different point. It was not losing money temporarily; in fact, it made a profit of $23 million. I said, "Why would they be closing down if they are making a profit?" I talked with the trade unionists, the mayor of the town, community representatives and the business people responsible for the mine. What did they tell me? They said, "Well, yes, we made $23 million profit, but if we take the $23 million and put it in the bank, we can get a 20 per cent return on that on a long-range investment without taking any risks at all in the marketplace, which we might have to do if we carried on with our mining business."
The situation of that one community is a good illustration of the lay-offs in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and elsewhere in Canada. On the one hand you have small businessmen who cannot carry inventory and will be forced into bankruptcy as a result of high interest rates, and on the other hand you have businessmen with capital to invest, but because they are not crazy they think it is more sensible to invest their money in the banks than to create jobs for Canadians. It is time to put an end to this absurd high interest rate policy, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then we come to the issue of home owners and renters, and that is perhaps the single most important category of people that certainly have been discussed in recent weeks. This group includes every Canadian, it seems to me, as the Liberals know. One is either a home owner or a renter. The government should be able to come to grips with that problem.
What has the budget done for these people? According to a document that we obtained some weeks ago, more than 100,000 Canadians are in serious difficulty in the coming year because they might lose their homes. That figure has moderated somewhat because interest rates and mortgage rates, which the government has allowed to follow market patterns, have decreased a little. However, the reality is that there are thousands, and if not 100,000, something close to it, facing serious difficulty. Why are they in serious difficulty? It is because they have to increase mortgages that are up for renewal.

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
This past weekend I was in Calgary and Saskatoon. In both those places the average increase in a mortgage renewal comes to $250 to $350 a month. To put it another way, $300 a month is $3,600 a year, and that represents a decline in one's living standard by that amount.
Mr. Cosgrove and the Liberal government say: "Oh well, there have not been many people who have experienced foreclosure". Of course not, Mr. Speaker, because the people of Canada, men and women who have put their life savings into their home, will not go through foreclosure. What they will do is take on an additional job and start to work 50 or 60 hours a week. Or if one partner in a marriage is not working, he or she will go to work. In some cases they have cut back on the kids' clothing budget or cancel vacations. Or as my colleague says, in most cases right now they cannot get another job because another job is not available. What does the budget do for them? The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and we were correct. It will provide assistance for some 2 per cent of the people faced with the terrible situation of losing their homes.
I should like to elaborate on how the government will provide this assistance. Are they doing it through our financial institutions? No, they will do it through loan guarantees provided by taxpayers, but they will only do it after, for example, a family with a mortgage of $50,000 who cannot keep its home defers the mortgage payments and goes more deeply into debt with the bank. Under this scheme, if one has a $50,000 mortgage and accepts the budget's recommendation, after paying for an entire year one will owe more on his house than he owed on the date of his initial payment. The government in its generosity to 2 per cent of the people threatened with losing their homes has forced home owners to become tenants in their own homes or permanent debtors, but has offered a guaranteed profit program for the banks.
Our solution differs from that of the government and the Conservative Party and is very clear in its difference. One group which has done very well with inflation is the banks of Canada. In the first nine months of this year the five major banks have had a profit increase of $1.5 billion. We must remember that 97 per cent of the mortgages in Canada are held by the banks, the trust companies and the insurance industry. As a democratic socialistic party approaching the banking system, in the housing crisis in particular but not restricted to the housing crisis, we say that in a mixed economy the banks can make profits in certain of their activities. It would be ludicrous from an economic point of view to offer a counterargument. Some of our cabinet colleagues across the way can afford a $175 per plate dinner in Toronto to raise money for the Liberal Party. If they or any Canadian wants to borrow money to go on holidays in Florida or elsewhere, to purchase mink coats or to put in swimming pools, let the banks charge them what they want. But when there is a housing crisis in Canada and according to the minister some 100,000 Canadians from coast to coast are threatened, since the banks had a $1.5 billion profit in the first nine months of this year,
surely it is time to think about what the Bank Act provided before the Liberals changed it in 1969.
Before 1969 the Bank Act fixed mortgage moneys at 9 per cent. The banks put up mortgage moneys; the ceiling was 9 per cent. Then it was changed. At that time one party in the House opposed the change-the NDP. The then minister of housing, Mr. Paul Hellyer, spoke in the House. I remember very vividly what he said. He said that they wanted to take out of the Bank Act the principle which set the then ceiling of 9 per cent. Also he said that they wanted to introduce what was then called for the first time the roll-over principle for mortgages. There used to be long 20 or 25 year mortgages. Mr. Hellyer for the Liberals said that they wanted to get rid of it and that it was being done for home owners. He said that was in their real interest.
Then he did two things. He took off the 9 per cent mortgage ceiling and allowed the banks and other financial institutions to put out mortgages which were renewable every five years. To those of us on this side who said that that would only guarantee the profits of banks, Mr. Hellyer said that we were wrong and, "There you are, you predictors of gloom and doom." He said that if the government introduced the roll-over principle there would be a great influx of mortgage money, that mortgages would come down and that home owners would benefit.
I should like to indicate what has happened with the rollover principle. Ever since it was introduced the banks of Canada have been rolling over home owners in the country; that has been the result.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We would say to all Canadian families who have to renew their mortgages at 18.5 per cent and upwards that they ought to be able to renew them during the next six months at the rates they are presently paying. The financial institutions can afford to absorb that. This is my first point. Second, we want to reintroduce the principle of social responsibility into the banking system. A New Democratic Party government would do the following within 24 hours. We would change the Bank Act and make it obligatory for banks to put up mortgage moneys at a level which average Canadian families can afford.
In terms of renters, if anything, the situation for renters in Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax or any urban centre will be worse than the situation for home owners next year. What has this imaginative Liberal government done? Has it indicated that there are more than one million unemployed in the lumber and construction industry, in the furniture, refrigerator and stove manufacturing industry, and that we should be doing something to stimulate employment? If the government had even thought that way, the conclusion would be obvious.
The government has announced that it will provide 15,000 additional units-its big increase-over the next two years. This will not even meet the needs of Vancouver, let alone all of Canada. The NDP say that with the present unemployment


November 16, 1981

The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
rate and with the housing crisis faced by human beings who need accommodation, there should be a massive increase in the Canadian housing budget to provide homes and rental accommodations for those who need them. Of course, this would provide jobs for the Canadians who would be building them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now I should like to deal with the interest rate argument in more detail than it has been dealt with in the past. When I was speaking at my party's convention in Saskatchewan, I was pleased to hear the Premier of that province say publicly that he was in agreement with what we had said about exchange controls. We think they are necessary now. I want to make the argument for them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I want to hear this.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear a member of the Conservative Party saying that he wants to hear the argument. I make the argument for the benefit of people on both sides of the House, and I should like to hear their replies. The Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada, as well as the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) as recently as last June in opposition, have indicated that we must keep raising our interest rate when the American rate is up or we will be in difficulty. We say that there is an answer. We can lower interest rates, but if we stop there those profound economic wizards in the Liberal and Conservative parties are correct that there would probably be an outflow of capital. We think we can go one step further. We do not just restrict ourselves to what social democrats have done around the world; we turn to the United States itself.
In the 1960s President Kennedy had an outflow of capital problem. What did he do? He established a system of controls on the export of capital to protect the American dollar for some time. Then in the 1970s when the well-known radical President Nixon was in charge of the United States, he had a problem as well. I do not think his office had been taken over by Trotskyites. He saw that there was a way to deal with an export of capital problem, so for a brief period of time he put export controls on capital.
We say that when farmers in Canada are going broke, when businessmen are going broke, when Canadians are losing their homes, if it was good enough for the Americans in the 1960s and 1970s to have controls on the export of capital, then it is good enough for Canada in the 1980s and it should be done.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. members for their indulgence.

I shall try to conclude quickly, Mr. Speaker.
There is one other point in the budget that I want to deal with before I turn the floor over to a Liberal member who, I hope, will reply to some of the arguments that have been made. This concerns the question of equity.
In his speech to the House and to the people of Canada on Thursday, the Minister of Finance made much of his party's alleged concern with fairness and with equity. I was touched by that. I heard in advance that they were really going to sock it to the rich. Then again, I thought that perhaps the Trotskyites had taken over the Liberal Party.
I listened with a great deal of interest to what was said in the budget about income distribution and tax benefits. Instead of that, we found that what the Liberal Party was doing with its left hand, it was busy undoing with its right hand, which is always much stronger. It closed some loopholes but left many more in place.
When you look at the tables and the charts that accompanied the budget documents you discover the following facts, Mr. Speaker. First of all, the vast majority of Canadians get no tax cuts at all. I repeat, the vast majority get no tax cuts at all. Second, a small number at the bottom of the tax scale get something like $4 per week. We are pleased that they get something but $4 per week is hardly the symbol of a government generous toward its people if you are living in poverty.
At the other end of the economic scale we find that there are 45,000 taxpayers in Canada earning $100,000 or more per year who, with this Liberal budget, will save $5,000 per year in taxes. We say that this is not tax reform, this is typical Liberal chicanery. The government tries to pretend that it is providing justice for all, but instead it is providing additional benefits for upper-income Canadians who need it least.
I will conclude with this observation, Mr. Speaker. What we need now and what we have needed for years is serious tax reform. As long as pensioners in Canada are paying taxes, as long as the working poor in Canada are paying taxes, surely to God it is time that the rich, the banks and the oil companies were paying their fair share.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was going to have something to say about how the government has abandoned its total commitment to the further Canadianization of our economy and how it has sold out the west and the western development fund, but my time is running out. I shall conclude with the following words, Mr. Speaker. More than ever before Canadians must know that there is one party in this land that remains in their corner, that there is one party that does offer heart and help and hope. I want to say to the Liberals and the Tories that they can take

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Deniger
their stand with the banks and we will take our stand with the ordinary people of this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Deniger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Multiculturalism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me to have an opportunity to take part in the debate on the budget which was tabled last Thursday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the three major themes of this budget cannot be overemphasized: restraint, equity and economic renewal. Indeed, the cornerstone of our government's budgetary policy is that it is vital that we should put an end to inflation if we want to reduce interest rates and tackle our other economic problems. Mr. Speaker, I plan to use the few minutes at my disposal to deal first of all with the immediate effects of the budget on Quebec taxpayers, especially those of the constituency of Laprairie of the cities of Saint-Lambert, Lemoyne, Greenfield Park, Bros-sard, Laprairie and Candiac, then, to comment on the various options which faced the Minister of Finance, and finally, to discuss the many contradictions in the attitude of the opposition members who addressed this budget, and God knows that we heard quite a few of them this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, voiced by both the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent).
It is important first of all to emphasize that by doing away with a great number of tax rebates, the government will be able to reduce the taxes that are paid by nearly 6 million taxpayers while increasing its revenue sufficiently to reduce the public deficit. For the Quebec taxpayers, in Canada, Mr. Speaker, these savings may be and are achieved in the following manner. First, the income tax rates for individuals whose income exceeds $ 11,000 will be reduced and the tax burden of individuals with lower incomes will be lightened. Those in the higher-income brackets will be encouraged to save and invest by the setting of a limit of 34 per cent for federal tax rates. The maximum tax rate will therefore be about 50 per cent, Mr. Speaker, depending on the provincial tax rate, rather than about 64 per cent as is now the case. The current tax reduction of 9 per cent will be replaced by a $200 credit granted to all taxpayers. Married taxpayers will be able to claim an additional $200 for a dependent spouse. This means that 620,000 lower income taxpayers will see their tax credit doubled or increased by $400. The indexing system provided by the act will remain the same, which will represent additional rebates of over $3 billion in federal and provincial taxes in 1982. The child tax credit will go from $261 to $293.
Generally speaking, personal income tax provisions for 1982, including the restrictions for preferential rates and indexation, will mean average individual rebates of $310 for nearly 12 million taxpayers, while approximately 795,000 taxpayers, most of whom have higher incomes, will pay more
federal taxes. A family of four will now be able to earn up to $15,000 without having to pay any federal income tax. In addition, in view of the lowering of unemployment insurance contributions, the net income of the wage-earning population will increase by $200 million. These tax incentives granted to all taxpayers are obvious and very important, but they mean even more, Mr. Speaker, for the Quebec taxpayer who is unfortunately governed in Quebec by a government known for its rather unhealthy administration.
Nonetheless, Mr. Levesque and the Parti Quebecois won the last election on the slogan of sound administration. Under a provincial Liberal government from 1970 to 1976, the average deficit of the government of Quebec was $451 million. Under the PQ it rose to more than $2 billion between 1976 and 1981. Between 1977 and 1981, the deficit increased 37.4 per cent under the Levesque government. The total indebtedness of the Quebec public sector went from $8,000 per family to nearly $15,000 in 1980. In 1980-81, provincial spending per capita were $2,700 in Quebec and $1,900 in Ontario. In the area of education alone, Mr. Parizeau recognized that in his 1979-80 budget Quebec was spending $500 more than Ontario per student.
In 1979, Mr. Parizeau discovered a $500 million shortfall in the department of education budget. He never succeeded in explaining that shortfall, and in the Quebec civil service, the remuneration per employee was $19,000 compared to $16,000 in Ontario. Clearly the Quebec taxpayer needs a sound fiscal administration, but he does not get it in Quebec. Quebecers are among the most heavily taxed citizens in America. The Canadian taxpayer with a $10,000 income pays $700 more income tax in Quebec than in Ontario. If he earns $20,000, the difference jumps to $2,000. Personal income tax in Quebec increased from $8.28 per $100 of personal income to nearly $9.50. The PQ government has just converted medicare, the automobile insurance board and Hydro-Quebec into tax collecting agencies. Not to mention the liquor board and all the other types of disguised taxes the government imposed on us Quebecers.
So, Mr. Speaker, I urge the PQ government to enter the federal arena. I invite them to come up with candidates against us. Of course, I wonder how they are going to call that group, whether it will be the Canadian Quebec Party or the Federalist Parti Quebecois, but I would urge them to do so because they should be made accountable.
In preparing this budget, our Minister of Finance was faced with the traditional economic dilemma facing every western democracy, namely to balance the demands of society for economic security with its need for economic growth and development. Of course, the answer is in our budget, that is equitable restraint. Over the last few weeks, Mr. Speaker, a number of groups from the municipal, provincial and federal
November 16, 1981

levels, a number of business groups, consumer groups, trade unions, home owners, renters and others suggested various fiscal measures to the minister for inclusion in his budget.
Unfortunately the common denominator of all those groups was indeed to reduce inflation, too often at the expense of all the other groups but not theirs. That is why the government must counter those inflationary demands with restrictive tax measures so as to maintain our anti-inflationary monetarist policy which, for awhile, was our only weapon to come to grips with the ever-escalating rate of inflation. Obviously the recent agreement between Alberta and the central government, and between nine out of ten provinces and the government of Canada with respect to both energy and the constitution will greatly improve the economic climate in Canada. Undoubtedly the fiscal measures introduced by the Minister of Finance in his budget last Thursday will bolster the dollar and lead to a definite lowering of interest rates.
An excellent example of inconsistent demand came from the ten provincial ministers when they were consulted about this budget last October. The provinces wanted the federal deficit reduced, of course, but none wanted the cuts to affect them. They all recognized that the most important fiscal measure we could take would be to reduce our deficit and our pressures on capital markets in order to fight inflation. But then most of them said that the federal government should not cut any revenue guarantees or transfer payments, should not raise or de-index any federal taxes, and should spend at least $800 million on a new federal subsidy program to protect all farmers, home owners and small-business men from the effects of high interest rates.
If they had the responsibility for balancing these conflicting demands for Canada's general economic progress on the one hand, and their own economic and political security on the other, perhaps they would recognize the desirability of phasing out the 1972 revenue guarantees in order to allow the federal government to reduce the deficit without affecting contributions to health care and post-secondary education. Perhaps they would recognize the need to end tax loopholes for the rich while reserving large cash expenditures on interest rate relief for those who need it most. In other words, they might be forced to make decisions about what is fair and equitable for Canada as a whole, instead of each demanding what is collectively impossible. That is what the Minister of Finance meant when he said that people must change their attitudes if inflation is to be beaten.

On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business recently made public its pre-budget review where it stated, and I quote:
-designed to dispel mistrust and uncertainties and to show the new way to follow.
Among other things, Mr. Speaker, the CFIB recommended that the $150,000 ceiling on the deduction granted to small-
The Budget-Mr. Deniger
and medium-sized businesses be raised to $200,000, and that the necessary amount of profits made by a business during all its operational life be increased from $750,000 to $1 million. This was approved. The CFIB asked for new unemployment insurance rules, so the budget provides for lower premiums for both employee and employer. The CFIB requested as well an extension of the Small Business Development Bond program for the expansion of small and medium-sized businesses and a wider field of application so that individual business owners might benefit from it as well. That proposition has been almost totally accepted.
The CFIB also urged the government to reduce federal expenditures and the share of government revenues now earmarked for servicing the debt. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that not only does the government intend to bring the deficit from $11.2 billion down to $9.8 billion in 1981-82 but it is also going to lower our cash requirements to $6.6 billion in 1982-83. We forecast a very sharp decline in our interest rates whose increase must drop from 38 per cent to less than 5 per cent if we are to pay our debt. It is important to recall that in our context of restraint and equity, the major requests of the CFIB have been met, even exceeded, and of course I am referring to the federal sales tax.

So, Mr. Speaker, do not misunderstand me. I am not criticizing Canada's economic interest groups for trying to protect themselves. Their leaders are elected or appointed to present a particular point of view. Their input into the decision-making process is invaluable; but all too often they make demands that are inconsistent from a social perspective, as if the pursuit of their own interests somehow automatically results in what is best for Canada as a whole.
The worst offenders are clearly the two opposition parties, for they are not supposed to be representative of particular interests. As national parties in a national parliament, they have a responsibility to reconcile conflicting interests and to balance conflicting demands for economic security and economic progress. That they have failed to accept that responsibility is plainly evident from the debate thus far. They are merely echoing the chorus of complaints.
Home owners and renters can be assisted in the long term by policies of fiscal and monetary restraint which will reduce inflation and interest rates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now comes the time to respond to both the NDP leader and the Tories. Let me start with the NDP leader. The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) clearly exaggerates when he accuses us of Canadianizing "Reaganomics". I believe the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) was sincere when he said that the greatest problem facing the Canadian people today was economic insecurity. But is that the whole story, and is the only way to deal with it to spend billions more dollars on government guarantees of economic security than we already do? Is that why his leader called a $350 million housing program a "puny response"?
However genuine the New Democratic Party's concern for equity and security is, it is inconsistent with, and undermined by, its $1.5 billion housing program and its artificial reduction of interest rates, which would increase the deficit, devalue the -dollar, fuel inflation and discourage capital from investing in this country and providing the jobs are so desperately needed.
This afternoon the Leader of the NDP told us about his great cure for high interest rates. In order to subsidize low interest rates, the NDP has proposed exchange controls to prevent large movements of more than $5 million out of the country. This would damage Canada's international image and jeopardize its economic relations by inviting retaliation. Foreign investors would stay away in droves. It is an example of how controls lead to more controls. Controls are their answer for everything except union wages. The NDP leader has even admitted that his party might consider exchange controls on average Canadians trying to transfer as little as $5,000 out of the country. Even Canadian vacationers would have their freedom of choice curtailed. That does not strike me as being the best way to provide equity and fairness.

The Progressive Conservatives also contradict themselves. Last October 4, Mr. Speaker, their financial critic said, and I quote:

This coming budget must pick first and foremost as its primary target and almost everything in that budget must be aimed at fighting inflation.
[ Translation]
Yet, last Thursday night, the same member suggested that the $50 million set aside for the Farm Credit Corporation was not enough and what was needed was $500 million. Mr. Speaker, if we had those $500 million, we would surely give them out, but as we all know that is over and above the entire
DREE budget and is an inflationary amount. The energy tax credit suggested by the hon. member is also an inflationary measure. You will also recall that the mortgage deductibility scheme supported by his party was not only inflationary, it was unfair and restrictive. When the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) speaks of a program that would apply to 220,000 housing units instead of 40,000, that is also inflationary.
The Leader of the Opposition was speaking earlier of other funding needs. He said that we should not have abolished some tax shelters because not only rich Canadians took advantage of them. Naturally, that is costly but still he wanted further tax credit measures, further exemptions and all sorts of tax shelters, even though the latter would have in fact prevented the government from collecting enough money to reduce its deficit and prevented over 6 million Canadian taxpayers from paying lower taxes.
I was keenly interested in the remarks made by some hon. members opposite a while ago when they said that we were the party of the banking interests and that we are in bed with them. And I find it still more surprising when I realize, just as all other hon. members of the House certainly do, that the deputy minister of finance who wrote the budget which caused the downfall of the previous Progressive Conservative administration is now a senior vice president of the Bank of Montreal. I certainly do not understand how hon. members of the Progressive Conservative Party would say all of a sudden that banks are Canada's worst enemies. It is a quite recent discovery. It is a sealed case.
We need only go over the questions which the members of the official opposition have been asking over the past few months to realize that they have no true economic policy and are trying every moment to please everybody. I should have thought, Mr. Speaker, that the experience in power of my hon. Progressive Conservative friends, however brief it was, would have made them understand. I should have thought, Mr. Speaker, that the Crosbie budget would have made them wiser. But no, Mr. Speaker; we need but recall the many economic debates held in this House to realize that their economic policy is as follows: Cut out everything except in my riding, which is utter nonsense, Mr. Speaker.
The problem facing the official opposition is also, to some extent, that which faces our society. Can economic growth and economic security go hand in hand? Professor Thurow of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology has written, and I quote:

Today, as never before, all policy solutions involve some degree of redistribution of income and wealth. And until we face up to this painful reality and learn as a society to agree on who should bear what costs, economic growth will continue to elude us.
That is the key to economic renewal, Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Finance so eloquently explained. Everyone, from the forester in British Columbia to the Conservative politician in Newfoundland, seems to be in favour of competitive eco-
November 16, 1981

nomics for others and protection for themselves. But this is Parliament and this is where the decisions must be taken. The buck stops here. It is no longer acceptable to make demands which are inconsistent. The challenge of government is to provide a balanced program of equity and restraint to ensure that we have both security and growth. And I once again congratulate the minister for meeting that challenge.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that under the present economic circumstances in this country as in the whole world, a budget is the most difficult working paper which a government is called upon to bring down. Due to the pressures brought to bear on a government, a budget introduced under the theme of restraint, equity and economic renewal is to the advantage of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be speaking today because the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) represents an expression of confidence in the ultimate strength of the Canadian economy. This budget sets its sights on the future and is laying the groundwork for the massive capital investment we will need in this decade and throughout the next to realize our development potential. The goals of this budget are not short term. The hon. Minister of Finance did not sacrifice long-term economic stability in Canada on the altar of short term political gain.
There can be no mistake. The major thrust of this budget is to meet the challenge of inflation, inflation which unfairly prejudices those on fixed incomes, inflation which erodes savings, inflation which exacerbates wage demands, inflation which decreases our productivity and international competitiveness, inflation which keeps interest rates high and which itself is fuelled by higher interest rates, each feeding voraciously on the other.
The single objective of this budget is to curb inflation and thus bring down interest rates. It does this by taking a large amount out of the budgetary deficit and thus out of the federal government's borrowing requirements. Last year the deficit was $1.5 billion less than had been predicted which, considering the high interest rates that we were required to pay, was welcome news to all Canadians. This year the deficit will be $0.4 billion less than predicted last year. It will decrease steadily in absolute dollar terms in the ensuing years. This means that as a percentage of our gross national product, the deficit will decline from a high of 4.4 per cent last year to 4.0 per cent this year and 2.8 per cent next year.
The leader of the New Democratic Party elaborately indicated to the House our major concerns about interest rates. The majority of his speech concerned the problems created by high interest rates. I had the impression that he was resigned to having high interest rates prevail in this country because he
The Budget-Mr. Peterson
believed that we should artificially force interest rates down and as enormous amounts of money flow out of the country we should stem the tide by imposing exchange controls and stopping it at our border. This approach has been tried in the past. He mentioned that it had been successful in the United States. In fact it did not work in the United States. First they tried the interest equalization tax, then in 1965 they tried the voluntary guidelines approach, and in 1968 they tried the mandatory guidelines approach. They finally had to abandon these measures in 1972. It has been tried in England and has not worked. It was tried in France-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are going to do it again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and it has not worked. Let us not think there is a magical solution which can bring down interest rates overnight, set up barriers and create a watertight capital market in order to protect us. What the government is doing in this budget is attempting to bring interest rates down by bringing down inflation.
The reduction of the government deficit will have an even more important impact on our financial requirements. The actual amount of money we will have to borrow will decline more rapidly from $10 billion last year to $9.7 billion this year. Next year the reduction will plummet to $6.6 billion. This represents a real reduction from 3.5 per cent to 1.7 per cent of our gross national product. I believe this is a responsible approach to take to deal with the deficit.

Mr. Speaker, substantial results are made possible thanks to two procedures. The first is a more adequate control of government expenditures. As it was pointed out by a few members, our economy is at a standstill. Consequently, it would be neither wise nor advisable to try to reduce the deficit by chopping drastically at government expenditures. It is essential that the rate of increase of most of our expenditures remain lower than the rate of growth of our economy.
That is why our expenditures will show a slight drop-in line with our economy-from last year's 20 per cent to 19 per cent in 1985-86. One reason why the public debt could not be reduced more substantially this year was the high interest rate which caused an increase in the public debt of $2.3 billion projected for last October. We must fight high interest rates, and we are using this budget and our monetary policy to do so.
The second means of reducing the deficit will be to increase revenue. Before the effects of the energy agreement are felt in two years' time, tax increases provided in the budget will generate additional revenues of $1.4 billion in 1982-83 and $2.1 billion in 1983-84, dropping to $1.2 billion in 1985-86.

These additional tax revenues are being derived in an important way. Reduced tax rates will apply to individuals with an income in excess of $11,120. Reduced rates plus a continuation of indexing will mean, for example, that a family of four with an income of $15,000 or less will pay no income tax. At the

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Peterson
higher end of the scale, the top marginal federal tax rate has been reduced from 43 per cent to 34 per cent. This means that the combined federal and provincial tax rates will fall from the present high of 64 per cent down to 50 per cent, and there will be a reduction of taxes on capital gains from 32 per cent to 25 per cent.
The budget undertakes the first major overhaul of our tax system since 1972 to make up for this lost revenue. This is accomplished by eliminating a number of tax expenditure plans, or loopholes, which generally benefit individuals in higher income brackets. The declared thrust of this overhaul is to create equity or fairness among taxpayers. The result of this is that some taxpayers in a higher bracket who benefited from these expenditure plans will face a net increase in their taxes.
I cannot help but recall some of the remarks made by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I would not have mentioned this had he not returned to this subject twice. He seemed to be quite concerned about the fact-and exercised about it-that the government was ensuring that individuals who used company cars for personal benefit would not get a tax break. He said that we were not penalizing fairly people such a travelling sales persons or real estate sales persons. What we are doing in this area is simply ensuring that that portion of their automobile which is spent for business purposes is not taxable, but if they use their car for pleasure, for example, to go to Florida by car for a vacation, that portion of it will be treated as a taxable benefit. Every other taxpayer has to pay for it. That is all we are doing. As the hon. member says, we are ensuring proper collection procedures in this provision. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition made quite an issue out of that. He said that if I was wrong he would expect me to vote for his amendment on this budget. But he did not have the courage to accept my counter offer that if he was wrong he would vote for our motion on the budget.

speechtext:
In the midst of these changes the budget has taken into account the devastating impact high interest rates can have on home owners who are facing the prospect of renewing their mortgages. A temporary system has been created combining guarantees and grants to ensure that home owners who might not otherwise be able to meet increased monthly charges will not be forced to sell their homes. Other measures have been designed to help small businesses and farmers to cope with the present high interest rates which we all agree are too high. For example, I believe our proposals regarding small businesses will bring them benefits amounting to an average of $27.5 million for each of the next two years.
Returning to the subject of interest rates, we must recognize that the help given to home owners, small business and farmers in order to allow them to cope with these high interest rates is only a stop-gap remedy. There can never be a real substitute for reducing inflation and thus reducing interest rates to a
reasonable level. We must ensure that the high rates do not again skyrocket.
I think it is important for us to recognize some important facts. Since August there have been ten successive decreases in the bank rate. It has come down from a high of 21.24 per cent to 16.13 per cent last Thursday, a decline of 5.11 percentage points. The prime lending rate has come down from a high of
22.75	per cent to 18 per cent, a drop of 4.75 percentage points. Likewise, the rate on five year mortgages has also declined
4.75	percentage points. I have not heard any approbation from hon. members opposite in this House as these rates have steadily come down. However, as those rates were going up, they criticized us. One would at least have thought that they would have been tempered and even in their distribution of praise and criticism. We recognize that the rates are still too high, which again dramatizes the need for measures which will bring down our rates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you taking credit for their falling?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope the hon. member will listen because, if he does, he might understand the full thrust of this budget.
As the Minister of Finance has said-and I echo his words here today-the foremost thrust of this budget is to control inflation and to keep bringing interest rates down. Let us look at the solutions offered by the Tories, who seem to be quite vocal this afternoon-through a rump group listening to the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), the Tory finance critic, one would think that he was in favour of our approach of reducing the deficit and bringing down interest rates, because he said this: "A manor drop in inflation and a major drop in interest rates is what this country needs most."
That was last Thursday. Thus far one would think that the hon. member is a fairly bright fellow. But wait; what he did after that was a complete U-turn. He criticized us by saying, "What we have is a restrictive budget when the reverse was called for." What he seemed to be saying in that last sentence was that he wants the government to enter into new expenditure programs, more government spending and a higher government deficit as a cure for inflation and high interest rates. However, 1 am not sure. That is what he seemed to be saying, but I am not sure because in another sentence he said that we should have been reducing the deficit even more. The only reasonable explanation for the U-turns and the contradictory statements by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre is that he wrote his response to the budget last September just after he was appointed finance critic. You should have seen the look on his face, Mr. Speaker, when he actually saw our budget documents and realized that our Minister of Finance meant real business in terms of dealing with inflation and high interest rates.
So much for the Tories. In terms of positive alternatives they are as bankrupt as they would make this country if we followed their proposals.
November 16, 1981

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like to address some remarks to the House concerning the tax provisions and changes dealing with charities. As hon. members are aware, the present system allows individuals or corporations to deduct up to 20 per cent of their income a year if they donate it to a charity. Any excess over the 20 per cent can be carried forward one year. The government has realized that this has not been adequate financial incentive to help the many individuals in this country who want to help the government assume part of the role of funding worth-while enterprises, so the budget has taken a very forward and far-reaching step and allowed donations in a year in excess of 20 per cent of income to be carried forward for five years. In addition, on death, donations exceeding the 20 per cent can be carried back for one tax year.
These measures are a constructive means to ensure that more of the burden of funding these worth-while and necessary institutions in our society is carried by the private sector. They are a direct encouragement to individuals and corporations to fulfil their responsibility to their fellow human beings in a way that no government institution could ever hope to emulate. I applaud the progressive steps of the Minister of Finance in this area.
In terms of social and economic development, many members of the opposition have said that we have not dealt with the question of development and that we do not have full provisions in the budget. However, if they read the documents tabled along with it, they would realize the commitment of this government to a full program of economic development. Let me give some examples. With respect to science and technology, research and development are at the heart of any industrial renewal. In terms of research and development the government has committed itself, in co-operation with the private sector, to reaching a level of 1.5 per cent of gross national product. To date we are already ahead of our commitment to reaching that goal. We have given over $1.5 billion this year. We have done it in a very constructive way in co-operation with the private sector. There is new funding for microelectronics centres in Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto, Sherbrooke and the Atlantic region. There is a new source development fund of $30 million to help Canadian suppliers of high technology goods and services. The Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council has an extra $20 million. There is an extra $27.5 million for application and marketing of Telidon Video-
The Budget-Mr. Peterson
tex technology. We have established an industrial opportunities program to co-ordinate existing programs, involving expenditures of $275 million annually. The government's work with Telidon has made it a world leader of which hon. members on all sides of the House are proud. I commend the department for setting up a $12.5 million program involving an office communication systems program. This is done in conjunction with companies such as Mitel. It will help increase white collar productivity, and we know that the number of white collar workers is increasing at a much faster rate than that of any other workers in our economy.
The Corporate Productivity Research Group includes Motel, Skyline Cable, The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and AES. This is an example of drawing together the strength of the private sector and the public sector to go on to new achievements in the fields of microprocessing and microtechnology. I believe microtechnology is important because it presents an incredible opportunity to create the new jobs which are going to be necessary in the future and and the extra productivity and social equity we want so that we can find, for example, more higher paying jobs for women.
In his remarks this afternoon the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition said we are not dealing with our economy seriously. He is wrong. The Minister of Finance is dealing with it seriously. The budget represents a long-term approach to reducing inflation and the high interest rates which are the root causes of our economic ills and concerns today. Let me demonstrate what type of confidence has been expressed in this budget. On August 4 the Canadian dollar was worth 80.31 cents U.S. Last Friday, after the budget, it was worth 84.09 cents. At noon today it rose to 84.32 cents. That is an expression of confidence. With a higher dollar we will be able to reduce inflation further, and that will make it possible to reduce interest rates. This was an expression of confidence in the budget by the international community and an expression of confidence in the direction being taken by this budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before getting into the main content of my remarks concerning the budget, I would like to refer to a couple of comments that have been made. It is quite astounding that members opposite are under the misapprehension that the people of Canada are sitting at home, reclining in their easy chairs, watching television as though the greatest thing to ever happen in their lives has happened.
Actually, these people are starting to wake up. They are beginning to put their chairs in a vertical position and are fast arriving at the conclusion that the budget has misrepresented to them the facts as they pertain to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
The budget brought down last Thursday night is nothing more than a blueprint for economic stagnation. As I proceed through my remarks, I will read into the record what the

November 16, 1981
The Budget-Mr. Domm
people in the ridings across Canada, both in the business and agricultural community, and home owners in particular, think about this budget and how it will affect them.
The government has spent a lot of time talking about restraint. In reality, it will be spending $13.1 billion more than it takes in. The people across Canada have reached the conclusion that for the government to have acquired over a period of a decade or more a debt of some hundred billion dollars with an interest payment to exceed $10 billion annually shows that it knows very little and practises absolutely nothing about restraint.
Another point made today regards the equity that appears in this new finance document known as our current budget. This budget is a bit of a sham. There is a lot of cover-up. People are beginning to realize that the higher income groups across Canada-and there are a lot of them as was stated by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) in his speech earlier-are the ones who will benefit from this budget. A lot of people in Canada earn $100,000 a year or more.
What is being done with that group of high-income people? Has the government taken from the rich and given to the poor? It has taken the 64 per cent tax rate of that group and lowered it. It has reduced the tax levied on high income people across this nation. The maximum personal tax that can be charged to that group has been set at 50 per cent.
It must be very difficult for a lot of Liberal Members of Parliament to return home and convince their constituents that this government has taken anything away from the rich. What it has done is to reduce their tax rate from 64 to 50 per cent.
Let us look at the fairness of this budget. A lot of deception can be read into the remarks by the Minister of Finance. This budget clearly and factually increases government revenues by 31 per cent while at the same time it will allow the government to continue to spend 22 per cent more than it did last year. It will be very clear to the people of Canada that the government is up to its old tricks. It is taking figures, juggling them, taking a little away here and a little away there. In reality, it very strongly favours the rich. I do not see much of a penalty imposed on the banks for the interest rates they derive or on high-income people who have had their tax rate reduced from 64 per cent to 50 per cent.
Let us look at what is in this budget for people in dire straits, those who were building up their hopes and expectations that the government was finally going to listen and implement a policy that would mean less of a financial burden in the coming year. What has been done for this group, namely, the home owners, small-business men and farmers?
First I want to deal with the home owners. I can speak with a reasonable amount of exposure to home owners, having been a real estate agent for a number of years. There is no doubt in my mind that the vast majority of Canadians who have scrimped, saved and invested in order to own a piece of Canada are in great jeopardy of losing that. It is not sufficient to tell those people that the government intends to address seriously the problem of high interest rates. This budget does
nothing more than subsidize the interest payments of a few hundred Canadians in some of the larger metropolitan areas in order that they will not have to spend more than 30 per cent of their gross income on interest payments for a mortgage.
There is a specific case in the constituency of Peterborough which has created a great deal of anxiety and concern for a home owner. The gentleman has allowed me to read into the record his specific situation. It clearly shows that what the government is offering home owners today is nothing new.
CMHC has followed the policy of advancing part of interest payments to home owners to tide them over a difficult financial period. I wish to refer to a specific case in my constituency.
In 1976, Mr. Tippet, a resident of R.R.2, Warsaw, took out a CMHC mortgage for $32,294. He required some assistance from the government in order to buy a home. CMHC arranged for AHOP assistance, assisted home ownership made easy. They advanced $3,200 to him since 1976 in order that he could reduce his payments.
The interest rate when the mortgage was renewed as recently as three years ago was 11% per cent. That is the interest figure I will use. It was lower than that in 1976. He has now added $3,200 to the original $32,294 mortgage and now owes $34,979. CMHC took a second mortgage for the $3,200. Mr. Tippet has to pay $342 a month. He went along with this plan from 1976 to 1981. They told him that the time has come for him to pay back the $3,200. They told him that they would like interest at the rate of 19'/2 per cent. I realize we are approaching six o'clock. I will complete my story later. We are now up to $34,979.
[ Translation]
